newsitem.title: DUBAI: Governments urged to open aviation markets.
newsitem.headline: Governments urged to open aviation markets.

text.p: Governments should open their aviation industries to international carriers and let market forces dictate, Susan McDermott, deputy director of negotiations at the U.S. Department of Transportation said on Monday.
"Rigid regulation cannot enhance customers' needs to move their freight nor airlines' needs to respond in efficient fashion," she told the 18th Air Cargo Forum in Dubai.
"Greater emphasis on market forces offers the...environment in which the international aviation industry has the ability to meet the challenges posed by new...economic world relations."
She said bilateral aviation agreements between countries "puts the concept of trade on its head" by telling producers what they can sell and consumers what they can buy.
"Too many governments have been making too many decisions... decisions that should be left to airline managements."
McDermott said the U.S. was party to about 80 bilateral aviation pacts, and there were now more than 1,000 worldwide.

These agreements contained some of the worst barriers to trade. "These walls governments have built around their aviation markets promotes isolation, inefficiency, economic stagnation, and impose huge costs on consumers and communities."
Liberalisation, on the other hand, benefited all. In less than two years after opening the U.S.-Canada market more than $4 billion in new economic activity had been produced, she said.

Ludolf (eds correct) van Hasselt of the EC's directorate general for transport said truly global carriers did not exist. But "in the next decade, aviation agreements between regions will replace agreements between countries, which will inevitably lead to more liberalisation".
McDermott said in some cases, a sectoral approach to liberalisation could be taken. Cargo operations were a prime candidate for this.

Federal Express Corp chief economist Ting Ho said the role of government in liberalising aviation markets would be increasingly important as international outsourcing -- which needed "a pipeline in the sky" to move goods -- was becoming But he said governments still had a lot to do in removing constraints to market competition and encouraging open skies.
